claims.text: An active-learning-trained MLIP can reproduce full fusion and high-temperature free energies in multicomponent high-entropy alloys.
The MLIP is calibrated using targeted ab initio molecular-dynamics data.
Training on solid and liquid configurations near melting will provide adequate coverage of the fusion transition.
Corrections or training data can retain vibrational entropy and electron–vibration coupling in the MLIP free-energy calculation.
CoCrFeNiTa is proposed as an example multicomponent HEA test system with equilibrium solid and liquid phases.
Active learning can automatically curate ab initio training configurations tailored to the target system and properties.
The training data will capture anharmonic effects, vibrational entropy, and electron–vibration interactions.
Simulation cells containing at least 256 atoms are large enough to capture configurational disorder and phase fluctuations.
MLIPs remove the conventional supercell-size limitation and facilitate configurational averaging in multicomponent alloys.
The MLIP implicitly samples the full free-energy landscape and encodes anharmonic vibrations, vibrational entropy, and electron–vibration contributions.
Actively selecting critical phase-transition configurations reduces the amount of required DFT data.
Spanning both solid and liquid phases in training allows the MLIP to learn the free-energy variations and entropy contributions governing fusion.
The trained MLIP enables rapid thermodynamic integration without prolonged AIMD while maintaining fidelity to subtle energy contributions.
MLIP-derived phase free energies and melting temperatures will have accuracy comparable to explicit AIMD and TOR-TILD.
The MLIP workflow will cost roughly one-tenth as much as explicit AIMD or TOR-TILD.
The method is applicable to typical multicomponent HEA compositions from near room temperature to the fusion point.
Success depends on adequately sampling solid states, liquid states, and critical transition configurations.
Performance may degrade when electron–vibration coupling or extreme anharmonic configurations are poorly sampled.
Deviation greater than approximately 10% in free energies, melting point, or entropy contributions, or failure to achieve an order-of-magnitude cost reduction, will falsify the hypothesis.
